summary: This memo defined the initial contents of the IANA Language Subtag Registry, used to build tags that identify languages. Because the content only seeded the registry, the actual list was removed before publication to avoid confusion with the live registry.

plainLanguage.summary: This was the starting list for a big dictionary of language names. Once the real dictionary existed, the starting list was taken out so nobody would mix them up.

subtitle: The IANA registry that provides unique codes for identifying languages, scripts, and regions.

tldr.problem: Web and Internet applications need a reliable way to identify and tag languages, scripts, and regional variants in a machine-readable format.
tldr.mechanism: The IANA Language Subtag Registry provides a centralized, standardized collection of codes based on existing international standards, allowing complex language tags like 'zh-Hant-HK' (Cantonese written in traditional script in Hong Kong) to be constructed from validated building blocks.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now reliably identify and process any natural language or script variant using standard, globally recognized subtags instead of ad-hoc naming.

today: RFC 4645 is Informational and is not obsoleted; it documents the initial population of the IANA Language Subtag Registry, which is still the authoritative source for language, script, and region codes used in language tags.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
Language tags are text strings that identify a specific language, dialect, script, or regional variant—for example, en for English, pt-BR for Brazilian Portuguese, or zh-Hant for Chinese written in traditional script. The IANA Language Subtag Registry is the authoritative source for the individual codes (subtags) that build these tags.

This RFC documents how the initial contents of that registry were populated. Rather than invent a new system from scratch, the registry reuses codes from four existing international standards: ISO 639 (language codes), ISO 15924 (script codes), ISO 3166 (country and territory codes), and UN M.49 (geographic region codes). This approach ensures compatibility with long-established naming conventions.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how a big, official list of language codes got its first set of entries. Instead of making up new codes, it borrowed codes from international standards that already existed.

sections.title: Subtags and Tags
sections.content:
A subtag is a single code element, such as en (English), Latn (Latin script), or US (United States). A tag is a complete identifier constructed from one or more subtags in a specific order: language, then optional script, then optional region, then optional variants. For example, zh-Hans-CN means Mandarin Chinese (zh) written in simplified script (Hans) in mainland China (CN).

The registry is formatted as records with metadata fields: a type field marking each subtag as a language, script, region, or variant; a description; and optional fields for deprecated codes or preferred replacements. The registry itself uses a modified record-jar format, a simple text-based structure suitable for parsing and distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: Subtags are like individual building blocks. A tag is when you put those blocks together to say exactly what language and place you mean.

sections.title: Building the Initial Registry
sections.content:
To create the initial registry, the authors applied specific rules to four source standards. For ISO 639 language codes, ISO 15924 script codes, and ISO 3166 country codes, they took all valid codes as of the date those standards were first referenced in earlier RFCs (such as RFC 1766). For UN M.49 geographic codes, they included only the macro-geographical (continental) region codes, excluding temporary groupings and areas not assigned an ISO country code.

Deprecated or withdrawn codes were marked with a deprecation date and a pointer to their replacement, but were not removed from the registry. This preserves backward compatibility: old tags that use deprecated codes remain valid but are flagged for users to migrate to preferred replacements.
sections.plainLanguage: The team went through each official standard and carefully selected which codes to include. If a code was old or replaced, they kept it but marked it as outdated and showed what to use instead.

sections.title: Migrating from the Older RFC 3066 Registry
sections.content:
Before RFC 4646 and its registry, RFC 3066 had defined an earlier set of language tags. The RFC 4645 process converted these older tags into the new registry format. Some tags, such as zh-Hant, became redundant—they could now be built from standard subtags already in the new registry. Others, like grandfathered tags (non-standard tags that had been registered and in use), were preserved as special records so that old applications would not break.

Variant subtags that appeared in RFC 3066 tags but were not yet recognized as standard codes became eligible for formal registration. The RFC lists a few such variants (for example, 1901 and 1996 for use with German dates). This ensured that legitimate historical tags could be migrated without losing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Old language tags had to be updated to use the new system. Some could be rebuilt from the standard codes, but special old tags were kept around so old programs wouldn't break.

sections.title: The Registry Today
sections.content:
RFC 4645 is Informational and defines the initial seed content, but the registry itself is now maintained by IANA as a living document. New subtags are added as languages, scripts, and regions are recognized; deprecated codes are updated when standards evolve. The registry file is publicly available and regularly updated, serving billions of web requests and applications that rely on consistent language identification.

The full registry is no longer included in the RFC itself (it was removed before publication to avoid confusion with the live version), but the criteria and process for initialization documented here remain the foundation for how the registry was bootstrapped and continues to be expanded.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gave the registry its first set of codes, but the list keeps growing as the world adds new languages and ways of writing. The real registry lives online where anyone can look it up.
